10.1029/2026gl123962.t: Detecting the Oceanic Moho Using Teleseismic P‐Wave Coda Autocorrelations of Ocean Bottom Seismograph Records
10.1029/2026gl123962.a: Abstract Although active‐source seismic methods can image the oceanic Mohorovičić discontinuity (Moho) at high resolution, their high cost motivates passive approaches using OBS, for which receiver functions (RF) are often complicated by instrument tilt, azimuthal misalignment, sedimentary layers, and water‐column reverberations. Here we apply teleseismic P‐wave coda autocorrelation to hydrophone data from OBS to image the oceanic Moho. Compared with vertical‐component data, hydrophone data provide a simpler interpretation because they avoid P‐to‐S conversions and are dominated by reflected and transmitted P‐wave energy. By analyzing autocorrelation results from 22 long‐period and 24 short‐period stations in the NoMelt experiment, we identify a Moho reflection with a TwTT of ∼2.56 s and resolve lateral variations in crustal TwTT that are smoothed out in the radially averaged representations of global velocity models. Combined with previous studies and model tests, this longer‐than‐expected crustal TwTT suggests that a crust‐mantle transition zone may exist beneath the NoMelt region.

10.1029/2026gl122406.t: Iceberg‐Generated Waves From SWOT: Disintegration of Iceberg A‐76A in the Southern Ocean
10.1029/2026gl122406.a: Abstract Amid rising global temperatures, icebergs are calving more often and drifting into open waters. Their disintegration processes can trigger energetic surface gravity waves that propagate away from the iceberg remain poorly documented. This study presents an analysis of 12 iceberg‐generated wave fields associated with the disintegration of iceberg A‐76A, utilizing sea surface height anomaly data from the Surface Water and Ocean Topography (SWOT) mission. We analyzed wave height, wavelength, depth regime, and Time Since Impact (TSI) using wavelet scalograms matched to dispersion curves. Waves fell within the linear intermediate‐to‐deep‐water regime, aligning with findings from Heller et al. (2019, https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598‐018‐36634‐3 ). Correlation found between steepness and TSI, as expected from theory. Preliminary results suggest the potential to infer calving mechanisms and direction from the scalograms. Despite SWOT's limited temporal resolution, demonstrates its unique ability to detect iceberg‐generated and novel view iceberg–ocean interactions, supporting future research with enhanced data and processing capabilities.

10.1016/j.rse.2026.115750.t: PACE hyperspectral observations enable a new paradigm for global mapping of terrestrial gross primary production
10.1016/j.rse.2026.115750.a: Accurate quantification of terrestrial gross primary production (GPP) is fundamental to understanding plant productivity, ecosystem function, and carbon-climate feedbacks. Existing approaches typically rely on meteorological, soil, and other ancillary inputs, which introduce substantial uncertainties at regional to global scales. NASA's Plankton, Aerosol, Cloud, ocean Ecosystem (PACE) mission, carrying the Ocean Color Instrument (OCI), provides the first contiguous global hyperspectral observations from space. Using 122 spectral bands from PACE, we developed a data-driven framework based on partial least squares regression to generate an 8-day global GPP product. The model achieves a robust performance (R 2 = 0.71, RMSE = 1.93 gC m −2 d −1 ), comparable to models that incorporate meteorological drivers, and outperforms approaches based on broadband reflectance or vegetation indices. PACE-derived GPP showed broad spatial correspondence with solar-induced fluorescence (SIF), including hotspots across high productivity regions such as the U.S. Corn Belt, the Amazon and Congo basins, and the Indo-Gangetic and North China Plains. This strong spatial coherence supports the physiological relevance of the PACE retrievals. Our results demonstrate that hyperspectral observations provide a direct, observation-driven framework for estimating plant productivity at the global scale, opening new opportunities for monitoring vegetation responses to environmental change.

10.1080/1064119x.2026.2755863.t: RANS-GPINN integrating residual-gradient enhancement and KAN for unsteady flow-field prediction around subsea pipelines
10.1080/1064119x.2026.2755863.a: This study addresses the slow convergence, limited representation of local high-gradient regions, and accumulation of boundary errors encountered by conventional physics-informed neural networks in predicting unsteady flow-fields around subsea pipelines. A RANS-GPINN model based on the RANS governing equations and integrating a residual-gradient enhancement mechanism with a Kolmogorov-Arnold Network (KAN) is developed for predicting the unsteady flow-field around subsea pipelines. The continuity equation, momentum equations, and turbulence governing equations are embedded into the training process, and residual-gradient terms are introduced in addition to the physical-residual constraints to improve the prediction accuracy for complex flow-field variations. A dataset for the flow-field around subsea pipelines is constructed from numerical simulations, and the effects of network depth, network width, and data normalization strategies are analyzed. The results show that a network with eight hidden layers and 64 neurons per layer, combined with full normalization, achieves a favorable balance among prediction accuracy, convergence performance, and computational cost. Compared with the conventional PINN-NS model, the RANS-GPINN model converges faster and provides stronger error control in complex boundary regions, reducing the maximum error from 0.0239 to 0.0111, a decrease of approximately 53.6%. Long simulations show better model stability, aiding turbulent load assessment on ocean engineering equipment.

10.3389/frsen.2026.1839175.t: AQUAVERSE-AC: a machine learning-based atmospheric correction framework for inland and coastal waters
10.3389/frsen.2026.1839175.a: Accurately deriving remote sensing reflectance (Rrs) from satellite imagery in optically complex inland and coastal waters is critical for water quality monitoring and management. This study presents AQUAVERSE (an aquatic inversion scheme for remote sensing of fresh and coastal waters), an innovative machine learning-based atmospheric correction (AC) framework, that leverages Mixture Density Networks (MDNs) to retrieve high-quality Rrs from multispectral data acquired by Landsat-8/9 (OLI) and Sentinel-2A/B (MSI) satellites. By coupling a well-validated ocean-atmosphere radiative transfer (RT) model with extensive simulated and in situ datasets, AQUAVERSE compensates for aerosol scattering and atmospheric absorption across diverse environmental and imaging conditions. The model’s performance was evaluated through a comprehensive matchup analysis against AERONET-OC and GLORIA datasets, wherein AQUAVERSE demonstrates substantial improvements over existing AC processors. Median residuals ranged from 15-26% for key spectral bands (coastal-blue to 705nm red-edge band), representing a 20-100% enhancement in accuracy compared to alternative methods. Notably, AQUAVERSE exhibited robust performance in the blue spectrum, where most AC methods underperform. The results, including generated Rrs maps, were benchmarked against outputs from other widely used atmospheric correction processors (ACOLITE, POLYMER, SeaDAS), demonstrating AQUAVERSE's enhanced performance across diverse aquatic environments, while also providing comprehensive uncertainty estimates. These uncertainty metrics, inherently generated by the MDN framework, provide critical confidence indicators for downstream applications. AQUAVERSE represents a significant advancement in atmospheric correction for inland and coastal waters, providing a reliable tool for monitoring water quality in diverse optically complex aquatic systems.

10.1080/15481603.2026.2751876.t: First results of joint sea surface salinity, temperature, and wind speed retrieval from MICAP Simultaneous L/C/K-band active and passive observations
10.1080/15481603.2026.2751876.a: The Microwave Imager Combined Active and Passive (MICAP) onboard the Chinese Ocean Salinity Satellite (HY-4A) is a novel spaceborne payload developed for the simultaneous retrieval of Sea Surface Salinity (SSS), Sea Surface Temperature (SST), and Sea Surface Wind Speed (WS). MICAP uniquely combines L-band (1.4 GHz), C-band (6.9 GHz), and K-band (18.7 GHz) one-dimensional (1-D) interferometric synthetic aperture radiometers with an L-band Digital Beam-Forming (DBF) scatterometer. This paper presents the Level-2 retrieval algorithms and preliminary validation results obtained during the early in-orbit verification phase of the MICAP ocean products. The retrieval framework adopts a two-step strategy, including an L-band only SSS retrieval scheme (Mode-1) and a combined multi-parameter retrieval scheme (Mode-2). In Mode-2, the simultaneous C/K-band measurements are first used to derive estimates of SST and WS. These auxiliary parameters are subsequently combined with the L-band radiometer and scatterometer measurements to perform the final SSS and WS retrieval. Preliminary validation against Argo observations shows an SSS RMSE of approximately 0.58 psu for the Mode-2 retrieval over the screened open ocean validation sample. The retrieved SST and WS products show RMSEs of 0.80 K and 1.17 m/s, respectively, when compared with iQuam and TAO buoy data. These results provide an initial in-orbit demonstration of simultaneous multi-parameter retrieval using the MICAP multi-frequency active and passive observations.

10.1038/s41612-026-01585-4.t: Generative assimilation and prediction for weather and climate
10.1038/s41612-026-01585-4.a: Machine learning models have shown great success in predicting weather up to two weeks ahead, outperforming process-based benchmarks 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 . However, most existing approaches do not fully integrate data assimilation into the prediction workflow 6 , 7 , and often suffer from error accumulation in autoregressive computation, limiting their applicability to predictions beyond the medium range 8 and climate projections 9 . We introduce Generative Assimilation and Prediction (GAP), a unified deep generative framework that connects data assimilation, weather forecasting, and climate simulation through a shared probabilistic representation of atmospheric states. GAP learns the climatological distribution from reanalysis data, and adapts it to different tasks by incorporating observational, predictive, and forcing constraints. Evaluated across a range of weather-climate tasks, GAP produces probabilistic weather forecasts competitive with leading forecasting systems, using its own assimilated initial states derived from 5% synthetic perfect observations, with particular skill in capturing extreme events such as atmospheric rivers, heatwaves and the Madden-Julian Oscillation. At seasonal timescales, GAP shows promising predictive skill when constrained by oceanic boundary forcing. Moreover, GAP supports stable millennial-scale climate simulations that reproduce atmospheric variability from daily weather fluctuations to decadal oscillations. These results suggest that generative modeling of the climatological distribution offers a viable foundation for seamless weather and climate prediction, thereby opening a path toward integrated, observation-to-climate workflows.

10.1071/mf26059.t: Trends in phytoplankton communities uncovered by the Southern Ocean Continuous Plankton Recorder
10.1071/mf26059.a: Context Phytoplankton communities in the Southern Ocean are shifting as the region experiences rapid environmental change. Aims To investigate long-term trends or changes in Southern Ocean phytoplankton communities, and model abundance patterns of key dominant genera against sampling year and sea-surface temperature (SST). Methods Using 10 years of Southern Ocean Continuous Plankton Recorder (SO-CPR) data within a 15-year period (2007–21), we examined long-term trends in phytoplankton composition, with emphasis on six ecologically important diatom genera (Chaetoceros, Thalassiothrix, Fragilariopsis, Pseudo-nitzschia, Rhizosolenia and Corethron). Key results Overall diatom and dinoflagellate abundances increased significantly across the sampling domain, whereas the diatom:dinoflagellate ratio remained stable, suggesting little change in the relative contributions of these major phytoplankton groups despite increasing overall abundance. Patterns among focal genera differed, with distinct temporal trends and contrasting relationships with sea-surface temperature, indicating ecological differentiation among dominant Southern Ocean diatoms. Conclusions No single genus accounted for the observed increase in abundance, suggesting a community-wide response to environmental change. Implications These results demonstrated the value of long-term CPR observations for detecting trends, natural variability and ecological change in a rapidly warming Southern Ocean.

10.3390/jimaging12110552.t: Conditional GANs for FL Sonar-to-Optical Image Transformation
10.3390/jimaging12110552.a: Underwater robotics platforms are equipped with onboard cameras for navigation and mapping within deep-sea environments, either assisted by an operator in human-in-the-loop missions or automatically through real-time processing of live video. The impairment of vision by turbidity can be addressed by deploying the recent generation of 2-D multi-beam forward-looking imaging sonars, but this comes with limitations; e.g., sonar video data are not readily interpretable by an untrained human operator and cannot be effectively processed by the state-of-the-art computer methods. We propose a framework to translate underwater sonar imagery into intuitive optical views. By training a conditional generative adversarial network (Nvidia Pix2PixHD) on paired clear-water sonar and optical datasets, our model can synthesize high-quality optical images from sonar data captured in murky conditions. Evaluations across two distinct datasets—testing variables like training size, image resolution, field of view, color relevance, and cross-device transferability—demonstrate that our approach performs robustly in practical real-world scenarios.
